newsitem.title: USA: Raytheon Corp. snares Hughes Electronics defense parts.
newsitem.headline: Raytheon Corp. snares Hughes Electronics defense parts.

text.p: Everything old is new again. Raytheon Corp., after it finishes swallowing GM Hughes defense electronics business sometime in mid-1997, will look a lot like the defense giant it was in the 1970s, analysts said Thursday.

"It is clear that the end of the Cold War, and the resulting decline in the U.S. defense procurement budget, have brought about fundamental changes to the defense industry requiring continued consolidation," said Dennis Picard, Raytheon's chairman, in announcing the deal valued at $9.5 billion.

Picard, 64, told a New York press conference that some of the 127,000 employees with the new company, including the Texas Instruments Inc. defense operations that Lexington, Mass.-based Raytheon bought earlier this month, will be cut or moved in a consolidation of some defense operations. But he expected the combined companies to have openings for 2,500 jobs, he said.

"Our hope is that, near-end, the amount of people we hire will offset the reductions we will have," he said, adding that he expected decisions to be made on Raytheon's commercial businesses -- appliances, aircraft and its Engineering and Constructor division -- in about two months.

Edward Jones analyst William Fiala said the deal will make Raytheon "a majority defense electronics company." Other analysts note the merger will mean Raytheon will have a lock on 80 percent to 90 percent of the missile business.
Picard reassured reporters anti-trust matters were "not a problem."

J.P. Morgan analyst Roger Threlfall said the Pentagon "is well aware of the overcapacity in the industry and there really isn't a problem with sole source providers. I can think of several examples -- aircraft carriers for one."
Raytheon spent the 1980s buying other companies, trying to diversify in an effort to shield itself from cuts in U.S. defense spending.

"But, if you look at that strategy from today's perspective in the defense industry, a flaw was revealed," Fourteen Research analyst Anthony Ginsberg said. "None of the companies they invested in is No. 1 in their field.
"With this and TI, they're not No. 1, but they're a player," he said, referring to Raytheon's deal to buy Texas Instruments defense electronics assets announced earlier this month.

But Fiala and Ginsberg said they thought Raytheon would sell off its Amana appliance division and possible sell or spin-off its $3 billion Engineering and Constructor division as well, which Picard has called a "trapped asset" or an asset whose value has been unrealized by Wall Street.
Raytheon's stock finished up $1.50 to close at $48.50, though analysts expect it to drop in the near future on a short term basis.
